questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{′}-4y=9{e}^{4x},
$$

has the complementary solution ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{4x}$, find the particular solution to the equation.

${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

We see that the right-hand side is $9{e}^{4x},$ and ${e}^{4x}$ is a term in the complementary solution, so we assume that a particular solution takes the form 

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{4x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

We calculate the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ using the product rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =(\alpha x{e}^{4x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha (x{e}^{4x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha ({e}^{4x}+4x{e}^{4x}) \\  & =\alpha (1+4x){e}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\alpha (1+4x){e}^{4x})-4\alpha x{e}^{4x} & =9{e}^{4x} \\ (1+4x-4x)\alpha {e}^{4x} & =9{e}^{4x} \\ \alpha {e}^{4x} & =9{e}^{4x} \\ \alpha  & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=9x{e}^{4x}.
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{′}+6y=30{e}^{-6x}+4{e}^{x},
$$

has the complementary solution ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-6x}$, find the particular solution to the equation.

${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

We see that the right-hand side is $30{e}^{-6x}+4{e}^{x},$ and ${e}^{-6x}$ is a term in the complementary solution, while ${e}^{x}$ is not, so we assume that a particular solution takes the form 

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{-6x}+\beta {e}^{x},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined.

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =(\alpha x{e}^{-6x}+\beta {e}^{x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha (x{e}^{-6x})^{′}+\beta ({e}^{x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha ({e}^{-6x}-6x{e}^{-6x})+\beta {e}^{x} \\  & =\alpha (1-6x){e}^{-6x}+\beta {e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\alpha (1-6x){e}^{-6x}+\beta {e}^{x})+6(\alpha x{e}^{-6x}+\beta {e}^{x}) & =30{e}^{-6x}+4{e}^{x} \\ (1-6x+6x)\alpha {e}^{-6x}+(\beta +6\beta ){e}^{x} & =30{e}^{-6x}+4{e}^{x} \\ \alpha {e}^{-6x}+7\beta {e}^{x} & =30{e}^{-6x}+4{e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients of ${e}^{-6x}$ and ${e}^{x}$ gives

$$
\alpha =30\,\text{and}\,7\beta =4,
$$

so, we have

$$
\alpha =30\,\text{and}\,\beta =\frac{4}{7}.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=30x{e}^{-6x}+\frac{4}{7}{e}^{x}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}-y=7{e}^{x},\,y(0)=4
$$

Given that the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{′}-y=7{e}^{x}
$$

has the complementary solution ${y}_{c}=A{e}^{x},$ solve the initial value problem.

$y(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

We see that the right-hand side is $7{e}^{x},$ and ${e}^{x}$ is a term in the complementary solution, so we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant to be determined.

We calculate the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ using the product rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =(\alpha x{e}^{x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha (x{e}^{x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha ({e}^{x}+x{e}^{x}) \\  & =\alpha (1+x){e}^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\alpha (1+x){e}^{x})-(\alpha x{e}^{x}) & =7{e}^{x} \\ (1+x-x)\alpha {e}^{x} & =7{e}^{x} \\ \alpha {e}^{x} & =7{e}^{x} \\ \alpha  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=7x{e}^{x}.
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{x}+7x{e}^{x}.
$$

We can find the constant $A$ using the initial conditions.

Substituting $y(0)=4$ into the general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A+0 & =4 \\ A & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=4{e}^{x}+7x{e}^{x}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{′}-3y=8{e}^{5x}.
$$

Find the general solution to this equation given that the complementary solution is ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{3x},$ where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

$y(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{3x},
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

We see that the right-hand side is $8{e}^{5x},$ and ${e}^{5x}$ is not a term in the complementary solution, so we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{5x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′}=\alpha {e}^{5x}\cdot 5=5\alpha {e}^{5x}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}5\alpha {e}^{5x}-3\alpha {e}^{5x} & =8{e}^{5x} \\ 2\alpha {e}^{5x} & =8{e}^{5x} \\ \alpha  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=4{e}^{5x}.
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{3x}+4{e}^{5x}.
$$
